title: Land Tenure Systems in West Africa
outline: Gift, lease and rental land tenure systems

modules.title: Meaning of Land Tenure and the Communal System
modules.html:
Meaning of Land Tenure

Land tenure refers to the system, rules and rights governing the ownership, control, use and transfer of land within a community or country. It defines who can use land, for how long, and under what conditions. In West Africa, land tenure systems have evolved from traditional customary practices to modern statutory frameworks, and understanding them is essential to appreciating the challenges and opportunities in agricultural land use.

Communal Land Tenure System

Under the communal system, land belongs collectively to the whole community, clan or village, and is held in trust by the traditional ruler, chief or family head on behalf of all members. Every member of the community has the right to use a portion of the land for farming or building, but no individual can sell communal land without the consent of the community.

Features of Communal Land Tenure

  • Land is owned collectively, not by any single individual.
  • The chief or family head allocates land to members based on need.
  • Land cannot be sold outright without communal consent.
  • Non-members of the community may only lease or rent land temporarily.
  • Unused land reverts to the community for reallocation.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Every member has access to landDiscourages long-term investment due to lack of individual title
Reduces landlessness within the communityCan lead to land fragmentation over time
Preserves cultural and communal valuesDifficult for outsiders to acquire land for large-scale farming

For instance, if a community's total land area is \(500\) hectares and it is shared among \(100\) households averaging \(5\) hectares each, but the population doubles to \(200\) households over a generation, each household's average allocation would fall to \(500 \div 200 = 2.5\) hectares, showing how population growth strains the communal system over time.

examples.q: A community owns \(800\) hectares of land shared equally among \(160\) households. If the number of households grows to \(320\) due to population increase, calculate the new average land size per household.
examples.a: Original average \(= 800 \div 160 = 5\) hectares. New average \(= 800 \div 320 = 2.5\) hectares. This demonstrates how population growth under a fixed communal land system reduces the average landholding per household, leading to fragmentation and reduced farm efficiency.

examples.q: State two advantages and two disadvantages of the communal land tenure system.
examples.a: Advantages: (1) Every member of the community has guaranteed access to land for farming, reducing landlessness. (2) It helps preserve communal and cultural values associated with land. Disadvantages: (1) Lack of individual title discourages farmers from making long-term investments such as tree crop cultivation. (2) It can be difficult for outside investors or commercial farmers to acquire large areas of land for modern mechanised agriculture.

modules.title: Inheritance, Gift, Lease/Rental and Islamic Land Tenure Systems
modules.html:
Inheritance (Family) Land Tenure System

Under this system, land is passed down from parents to children or other relatives according to customary or family rules. This is the most common way individuals acquire farmland in many West African societies. Over successive generations, however, continuous subdivision of the family land among many heirs results in fragmentation, with each heir receiving a progressively smaller and often scattered portion.

Gift Land Tenure System

Land may be given outright as a gift by a landowner to another person, often as a reward for service, as a form of appreciation, or to a religious institution. The recipient of a gift of land typically gains full rights of use, though in some customary settings, the original family retains some residual interest.

Lease and Rental Land Tenure Systems

Under a lease, land is given to a tenant for a specified period in exchange for an agreed payment, either as a fixed cash rent or a share of the produce (share-cropping). For example, if a tenant leases \(4\) hectares of land at \(\text{N}\,25{,}000\) per hectare per year, the total annual rent is \(4 \times 25{,}000 = \text{N}\,100{,}000\). In share-cropping, if the agreement is for the tenant to give the landlord \(30\%\) of harvested produce and the tenant harvests \(2000\) kg of yam, the landlord receives \(0.30 \times 2000 = 600\) kg.

Land Tenure Under Islamic Law

In many parts of Northern Nigeria and other Muslim communities in West Africa, land tenure is influenced by Islamic law (Sharia), where land ultimately belongs to Allah but is held in trust by the ruler (Emir) who allocates it to subjects. Individuals have strong rights of use and can also inherit land according to Islamic inheritance rules, which specify fixed shares for different relatives.

SystemBasis of Access
InheritanceFamily relationship
GiftVoluntary transfer by owner
Lease/RentalPayment of rent or produce share
Islamic systemAllocation by ruler under Sharia principles

examples.q: A tenant leases \(6\) hectares of farmland at \(\text{N}\,18{,}000\) per hectare per year. Calculate the total annual rent payable.
examples.a: Total annual rent \(= 6 \times 18{,}000 = \text{N}\,108{,}000\). This is a fixed cash rent arrangement under the lease/rental land tenure system.

examples.q: Under a share-cropping arrangement, a tenant agrees to give the landlord \(25\%\) of harvested cassava. If the tenant harvests \(3200\) kg, calculate the landlord's share and the tenant's remaining share.
examples.a: Landlord's share \(= 0.25 \times 3200 = 800\) kg. Tenant's remaining share \(= 3200 - 800 = 2400\) kg. This illustrates how produce-sharing arrangements distribute farm output between landlord and tenant based on an agreed percentage.

modules.title: Problems of Land Tenure Systems and the Land Use Act of 1978
modules.html:
Problems Associated with Traditional Land Tenure Systems

  • Land fragmentation: continuous inheritance-based subdivision creates uneconomically small farm units.
  • Insecurity of tenure: tenants and borrowers of land have no guarantee of continued access, discouraging investment.
  • Land disputes and litigation: unclear or overlapping boundaries between families and communities often lead to costly and prolonged court cases.
  • Difficulty for large-scale investors: communal ownership structures make it hard for government or private investors to acquire large contiguous areas of land for commercial agriculture.
  • Gender inequality: in many customary systems, women have limited or no rights to inherit or independently own land.
  • Underutilisation: some landowners hold on to large idle portions of land for speculative purposes rather than productive use.

The Land Use Act of 1978

To address these problems, the Federal Government of Nigeria promulgated the Land Use Act in 1978, which vested ownership of all land in each state in the hands of the Governor, who holds it in trust for the people. Under this Act, individuals and communities are granted a Certificate of Occupancy (C of O), which gives legal rights of use for a specified period, typically \(99\) years, rather than outright ownership.

Objectives and Effects of the Land Use Act

  1. To make land more easily accessible to individuals and organisations, including for agricultural purposes.
  2. To reduce speculative land dealings and hoarding of land.
  3. To simplify and unify the previously diverse and often conflicting customary land tenure practices.
  4. To provide a legal basis (Certificate of Occupancy) for using land as collateral for loans.
FeatureDescription
OwnershipVested in the State Governor in trust for the people
Document of titleCertificate of Occupancy (C of O)
DurationTypically 99 years, renewable

Despite its good intentions, the Land Use Act has faced criticism for slow and bureaucratic processes in obtaining a Certificate of Occupancy, and for still not fully resolving disputes rooted in customary claims. If it takes an average of \(2\) years to process a C of O application and a farmer needs land urgently for a seasonal crop, this delay can significantly discourage timely agricultural investment.

examples.q: Explain the main purpose of the Certificate of Occupancy under the Land Use Act of 1978, and state its typical duration.
examples.a: The Certificate of Occupancy (C of O) is a legal document granted to individuals or organisations that gives them the right to use land for a specified purpose, typically for a duration of \(99\) years. It does not confer outright ownership since land ownership is vested in the state Governor, but it gives the holder secure, legally recognised rights of use, including the ability to use the land as collateral for obtaining loans.

examples.q: State three problems commonly associated with traditional land tenure systems in West Africa.
examples.a: (1) Land fragmentation, where continuous inheritance-based division results in very small, scattered plots unsuitable for mechanised farming. (2) Land disputes between families or communities due to unclear boundaries, often leading to costly litigation and abandonment of farmland. (3) Gender inequality, where women in many customary systems are denied independent rights to inherit or own land, limiting their participation in commercial agriculture.

options: the type of crops grown on land
the system of rules governing ownership, control and use of land
quiz.solution: Land tenure defines who owns, controls and can use land, and under what conditions, within a community or country.

quiz.q: Under the communal land tenure system, land is owned by
quiz.solution: Communal land tenure vests ownership collectively in the community, clan or village, held in trust by the chief or family head.

quiz.q: A community with 600 hectares shares it equally among 120 households. If households increase to 200, the new average land size per household is
The most common way individuals acquire farmland traditionally in West Africa is through
quiz.solution: Inheritance (family) land tenure is the most widespread traditional method of acquiring farmland.

quiz.q: A tenant leases 5 hectares at N20,000 per hectare per year. The total annual rent is
Under a share-cropping agreement, a tenant gives 20% of a 2500 kg yam harvest to the landlord. The landlord receives
In many Northern Nigerian Muslim communities, land tenure is influenced by
quiz.solution: Islamic land tenure principles, where land is held in trust by the ruler and allocated to subjects, are common in many Muslim communities in West Africa.

quiz.q: A major problem of the inheritance land tenure system is
options: land fragmentation into small uneconomical plots
quiz.solution: Repeated subdivision of family land among heirs over generations results in fragmentation into small plots.

quiz.q: The Land Use Act was promulgated in Nigeria in the year
quiz.solution: The Land Use Act was enacted in 1978 to reform land ownership and administration in Nigeria.

quiz.q: Under the Land Use Act, ownership of land in each state is vested in
options: the State Governor, in trust for the people
the Federal Ministry of Agriculture alone
quiz.solution: The Act vests all land in each state in the Governor, who holds it in trust on behalf of the people.

quiz.q: The legal document granted under the Land Use Act to give an individual rights to use land is called
quiz.solution: The Certificate of Occupancy (C of O) grants legally recognised rights of use over land, typically for 99 years.

quiz.q: A key objective of the Land Use Act was to
options: reduce speculative land dealings and simplify access to land
abolish all customary land rights immediately
prevent the use of land as collateral
quiz.solution: The Act aimed to reduce hoarding/speculation and make land access more uniform and straightforward across the country.

quiz.q: A common criticism of the Land Use Act is that
options: the process of obtaining a Certificate of Occupancy can be slow and bureaucratic
it has completely eliminated land disputes
it gives women full equal land rights everywhere
quiz.solution: Despite its aims, the bureaucratic delay in processing C of O applications remains a notable criticism of the Act.

quiz.q: Gender inequality in land tenure mainly refers to the fact that
options: women in many customary systems have limited rights to inherit or own land
children automatically own all family land
foreigners have more land rights than citizens
quiz.solution: In several customary systems, women face restrictions on independently inheriting or owning land, limiting their agricultural investment opportunities.

quiz.q: If it takes 2 years on average to process a Certificate of Occupancy, the main agricultural consequence for a farmer needing land urgently is
quiz.solution: Long processing times for legal land documents can delay a farmer's ability to invest in land improvements or begin seasonal cropping on time.
